newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Belgian money yld spread on Germany seen narrowing.
newsitem.headline: Belgian money yld spread on Germany seen narrowing.

text.p: The premium of Belgian money market yields over German rates should narrow in the months ahead, but the spread of Belgian bonds over Bunds is set to stick at current levels, economists said on Tuesday.

Belgium's short-term yield spread over Germany, which had hovered around zero for much of 1996, shot up to more than 100 basis points in March as Belgium's centre-left government was rocked by allegations of bribes paid to politicians in the late 1980s to secure defence contracts.

Although the survival of the coalition had never been seriously at stake and the scandal has since blown over, benchmark Belgian three-month yields have remained stubbornly 15 to 35 bp above equivalent German yields.
"The high short-term yield spread cannot be explained by economic fundamentals. It is probably a temporary situation," Bacob Bank market economist Wim Melyn told Reuters.
BBL economist Kristin Vandenbergen agreed. "The short-term yield spread (over Germany) is abnormally wide. There is no reason for this and we expect it to come in."
Benchmark Belgian three-month T-bill yields were quoted 3.28/30 percent in afternoon trade, compared to 3.06/12 percent for German three-month yields.
Most economists polled expected Belgian money market and bond yields to trend slightly higher in the second half of 1997, but they expect the yield curve will keep its steep 250 bp slope.
Forecasts for three month yields by end December range between 3.00 and 3.40 percent, while 10-year bond yields are seen between 6.00 and 6.10 percent from the current 5.63 percent.
The OLO/Bund spread was seen sticking to its narrow 5-10 bp range until year end, unless there would be a major upheaval in markets due to Europe's single currency project.

With its 1997 budget deficit firmly on track for 2.8 percent of GDP and 1998 deficit targets at 2.5 or possibly 2.3 percent, there was little doubt that Belgium would join the single currency if and when it happens in 1999, the analysts said.
But any talk of a delay to the euro's coming could take a heavy toll on Belgian debt markets.
"If EMU did not take place, then markets would start looking at Belgium's debt again," said Milan Khatri of London-based fixed-income research company Wrightson Associates.
Belgium's debt, at 130 percent of GDP in 1996, is the highest of the 15 EU countries.
"If there is any doubt that EMU would not be on time, there will be pressure on the franc," Khatri added.
Generale Bank chief economist Peter Praet said that September, when several European countries including Belgium draw up their 1998 budgets, could be a crucial period.
"The danger for Belgium is not so much the Belgian budget, but the French budget," Praet said, adding that an unconvincing French 1998 budget could have a domino effect on Belgium.
